members.name: accordion

coordinates with the one it is in now. `closest` crosses no shadow
boundary, which is correct: an item inside another item's content is in
that item's light DOM and finds the same accordion, so the check below is
what keeps it independent.

members.name: peers

Direct children only. An accordion nested inside an item's content is a
separate set, and opening a section in it must not close anything outside.

members.name: handleToggle
members.description:
Opens or closes this item, and enforces the accordion's mode.

The item that was clicked is the coordinator. It refuses first, then
announces, then applies, then closes its peers, in that order: closing a
peer before knowing whether this change was even allowed would leave the
set collapsed after a listener refused it.

members.name: focusTrigger
members.description:
Moves focus to this item's trigger.

The parent accordion drives arrow-key navigation and cannot reach the
trigger itself, because it is inside this item's shadow root. Exposing the
intent as a method keeps the parent out of the child's internals.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: onOpenChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the state is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. And not reachable from React's JSX,
which reserves every `on[A-Z]` prop for its own event system and drops
what it does not recognize; the generated wrapper listens for the events
instead.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

has to remember to include it.

declarations.description:
Holds the mode and nothing else. The item that was clicked is what
coordinates: it walks up to the nearest accordion, reads the mode off it, and
closes its peers itself.

Coordination is structural, not a subscription. `helix-open` does not bubble
and is not composed, because overlays nest and an inner one's lifecycle must
never read as the outer one's, so an accordion cannot learn that a child
opened by listening for it.

Membership resolves on demand, so there is no registry to keep in step: an
item added a second after render coordinates on its first click.

Items are matched with `instanceof HelixBaseAccordionItem`, never by tag
name. Matching `helix-accordion-item` would tie this tier to the styled one.

Every listener is attached on connect, so none of it runs on the server,
where there is no tree to walk and no events to hear.

members.name: mode
members.description:
How many sections may be open at once.

Absent is `multiple`, so nothing closes unexpectedly and the default costs
no attribute on the host. `single` keeps exactly one open and refuses to
close the last; `single-collapsible` keeps at most one and lets it close.

A union rather than a mode plus a `collapsible` boolean, which would make
`collapsible` alongside `multiple` expressible and meaningless.

declarations.description:
Chrome rather than content. An announcement sits above the header and speaks
for the whole page: a trial ending, a service degraded, a change of terms. A
passage that interrupts a document to set itself apart is a `Callout`, which
is read where it sits and cannot be dismissed. Neither is a variant of the
other.

**Always a polite live region.** `role="alert"` is assertive and interrupts
whatever is being read, which is right for something that appears mid-session
and wrong for something that was in the served HTML: an assertive
announcement would cut across a screen-reader user on every page load, before
they had read anything. Politeness costs a moment and is never wrong; the severity
does not change that, because an error that was always there is still not an
interruption.

Dismissing is a request. The announcement does not remove itself, because the
consumer owns the markup and taking the node out from under them would put
their state and the document out of step. `preventDefault()` on the
`helix-dismiss` is a refusal.

declarations.description:
Tracks whether the page has scrolled and reflects it as `data-scrolled`, so
the styled tier can lift the bar off the page without a scroll handler of its
own. Scroll position is the one piece of state the server genuinely cannot
know, so it is read on connect rather than derived: a fresh load starts at
the top, which is what the server rendered, and a reload part-way down
corrects on hydration.

The listener is passive and reads `scrollY` only, so it never blocks
scrolling.

Three regions, each in its own wrapper, because the row is a grid and a grid
needs three items to put the middle one in the middle. A bare slot is
`display: contents`, so its assigned elements become grid items themselves:
two actions would take two tracks and push the navigation off center. These
wrappers earn their boxes, which is the test; they carry no inset or fill of
their own, so an empty one still paints nothing.

The host is the banner and spans the viewport; the row inside it is what gets
centered. A banner that is itself narrowed leaves its background stopping
short of the window edges, which reads as a floating bar rather than as the
top of the page. That needs one element and one row, not a wrapper as well:
the host carries the material and `content` carries the measure.

left over, so the middle of the nav is the middle of the window whatever

declarations.description:
A part of `Avatar` rather than a family of its own: it arranges avatars and
is about nothing else, and its member is a complete `Avatar` the group did
not have to explain.

**The overflow count is the group's, not a slot.** Which avatars are hidden
is a fact the group works out from `max` and how many it was given, so a
consumer writing the "+3" themselves would be writing a number that has to
agree with a list they do not control.

**Hidden, not removed.** Past `max`, the extra avatars stay in the DOM and
stop being shown, so nothing re-renders when `max` changes and the accessible
name can still be built from all of them. The count is what a sighted reader
gets; the group's own name is what everyone else gets, and "Seven people" is
more useful than seven names read in a row.

**It is a list.** A row of faces is a set of separate people, and a group
with no role announces as one run of text. `role="list"` needs its children
to be `listitem`, which they cannot be told to become without writing an
attribute onto a consumer's element, so the group carries `role="group"` and
its name instead: one announcement, correct, and nothing written to anyone
else's markup.

declarations.description:
Wraps whatever it decorates and pins the indicator to its corner, so the
thing being counted stays the thing in the layout: a badge is an annotation,
not a container that happens to hold an icon.

The indicator says how many, and none is none. A `value` that reads as zero
shows no mark at all, an absent one shows a bare dot, and any other value
shows the value. `max` caps the top: past it the indicator reads `{max}+`
rather than growing to fit, since a corner mark that widens with its value
pushes the layout around.

**A dot needs a label.** Without one it is a colored circle that announces
nothing, which tells a sighted reader there is something new and tells
everyone else there is not. The label is required in that form, and the
indicator is hidden from assistive technology when a number already says it.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

the structure the HTML spec describes for exactly this: the attribution is

members.description:
Says on the footer whether there is an attribution in it.

A `<footer>` with nothing in it is still a block in the quote's flow and
still takes the container's gap, so every blockquote written without an
attribution reserved a full space below itself. There is no selector that
can ask, `slot:empty` being about a slot's fallback rather than its
assigned nodes, so the component asks and says so on the footer inside this
shadow root: an attribute on the host is a change to markup the consumer
rendered, which React reports on hydration.

declarations.summary: Groups related buttons into one control.

declarations.description:
Renders a real `<button>`, so activation, focus, and the browser's own
affordances come from the platform rather than from key handlers.

**It never renders an anchor.** A router has to render its own `<a>` to
intercept a click and cannot render one inside this shadow root, so a button
that could also be a link forced every such navigation to be a full page
load. A link that looks like a button is styling rather than behavior, so it
is a recipe in the base layer: `<Link data-button="primary">` is the same
control, and the consumer keeps their anchor.

`delegatesFocus` puts focus on the inner control, and it serializes into the
server's markup, so the button is keyboard reachable before any JavaScript
loads.

Form submission is explicit. A `<button type="submit">` inside a shadow root
submits nothing, because the form is on the other side of the boundary, so
the inner control is always `type="button"` and this element calls
`requestSubmit()` on its form instead. That routes through validation, unlike
`submit()`.
declarations.name: HelixBaseButton

slots.description: Content before the label, usually an icon.
slots.name: start

members.name: type
members.description: What activating the button does to its form.

members.name: label
members.description:
Accessible name, for a button whose content is not text.

Lives here rather than only on `IconButton` so the two share one render.
An icon-only button without it is a control a screen reader announces as
"button" and nothing else.

members.name: command
members.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

members.name: commandFor
members.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Moves focus to the inner control, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: focusable
members.description:
Whether the button holds its group's tab stop.

A toolbar keeps one tab stop across its children, and the obvious way to do
that is to write `tabindex` onto each of them. That is a change to markup
the consumer rendered, so a React consumer's hydration reports it and does
not patch it up. A parent sets this property instead, which writes nothing,
and the stop lands on the inner control inside the shadow root.

No attribute, because it is coordination between elements rather than
anything a consumer sets.

members.name: linkCommand
members.description:
Points the inner button at the command's target, by reference.

**The attribute cannot do this and it fails silently.** `commandfor` is an
IDREF, and an IDREF resolves inside the tree it is written in: forwarded
onto a button in this shadow root it looks for the id *here*, finds
nothing, and the trigger does nothing at all. Measured before this existed:
the button clicked, no `command` event was dispatched, and there was
nothing anywhere to say why.

`commandForElement` takes an element instead, and an element reference
resolves outward: a node in a shadow root may point at one in the document.
The same asymmetry the listbox relies on for `aria-activedescendant`, and
the second place in this library where the id form is the one that cannot
work.

The id is looked up in the host's own root rather than the document, so a
button inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root
and not a coincidence in the page.

members.name: commandTarget
members.description:
The element this button commands, or nothing.

Looked up in the button's own root rather than in the document, so a button
inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root and not
a coincidence in the page.

members.name: sendCommand
members.description:
Sends the `command` event where the browser will not.

Invoker commands are recent, and where they are missing `linkCommand` set a
property that does not exist and returned, so the button did nothing at all
when clicked. Silently: the markup was right, the component was right, and
every `command` in the library was inert at once with no error to find. A
design system cannot ship an example that depends on a feature failing that
quietly.

Only where the platform is absent, so a browser that has invokers sends
exactly one event and this sends none. Doing both would open a dialog and
immediately toggle it shut again, which is a worse bug than the one this
fixes and would only appear on the browsers that work.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description: The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

declarations.summary: Triggers an action, submits a form, or navigates.

declarations.description:
A grid of days, per the APG date grid: the whole grid is one tab stop, arrows
move by day and week, `PageUp` and `PageDown` move by month, and `Home` and
`End` go to the ends of the week. Only the focused cell is in the tab
sequence.

Roving `tabindex` is written on the cells, which is free here because they
are rendered into this shadow root rather than being markup a consumer wrote.

Dates are `YYYY-MM-DD` strings and every calculation is in UTC. A local-time
`Date` shifts across a timezone or a daylight-saving boundary, so the string
is what the component holds and the arithmetic never leaves UTC.

`month` is what the grid shows, separately from `value`, so paging through
months does not select anything and a consumer can drive the view. Left
unset, it follows the first selected date, and then the current month.

`mode` decides how many dates are held. Absent takes one. `range` takes two
and marks everything between them, starting over on the third click rather
than replacing an end at random. `multiple` toggles, so clicking a chosen
date takes it out. All three read and write the same comma-separated
`value`.

`locale` is worth setting where the output is compared across environments.
Left unset, month and day names come from the runtime's own locale, and a
server and a browser need not agree on what that is.

members.description: Dates that cannot be chosen, comma separated, as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

members.name: disableDays
members.description: Days of the week that cannot be chosen, comma separated, `0` to `6`.

members.name: month
members.description:
The month on show, as `YYYY-MM`. Follows `value`, then the current month.

Separate from `value` on purpose, so paging selects nothing and a consumer
can drive the view. It said that and could not do it: the calendar wrote
this when the reader paged, so a consumer holding it was overwritten and
never told. Reading gives the month on show; writing declares it theirs,
and `default-month` seeds one the calendar owns.

Accessible name for the control that pages back.

A property because this is the one component in the library that takes a
`locale`, and it carried two hardcoded English names with no way to change
them: a calendar rendering its own month names in Japanese still announced
its controls in English. `attribute:` spelled out, since Lit lowercases a
camelCase name rather than dash-casing it.

members.description: Month to open on, where nothing declared one.

members.description: The month on show, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: monthMode
members.description: Whether the consumer owns the view, decided once and then fixed.

members.name: min
members.description: Earliest selectable date, as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

members.name: max
members.description: Latest selectable date, as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the grid.

members.name: firstDayOfWeek
members.description: First column of the week, `0` for Sunday through `6` for Saturday.

members.name: focused
members.description: The date the grid's tab stop is on. Absent until the grid is used.

members.name: selected
members.description: The selected dates, in order.

members.name: range
members.description: The range's ends, when there are two and the mode asks for them.

members.name: shown
members.description: The month being shown, resolved from `month`, then `value`, then today.

members.name: derivedMonth
members.description:
The month to open on when nothing has declared one.

Split out from `shown` so `month` can report what is on display without the
two calling each other: `month` reading `shown` and `shown` reading `month`
is a stack overflow, and the specs found it immediately.

members.name: anchor
members.description:
The date the tab stop sits on, which is where the arrows move from.

It has to be a date the grid actually renders, so the month is compared
with its year. Comparing the month alone puts the stop on the same date a
year away, which is rendered nowhere, and the grid is left with no tab stop
at all and no way into it from the keyboard.

Each candidate is tested in turn rather than the first one winning
outright. Where the last date focused is in some other month, the selected
date still holds the stop, and only with neither in view does it fall to
the first of the month.

members.name: weeksOf
members.description: Six weeks of dates, so a grid does not change height between months.

members.name: barred
members.description:
Whether a date is barred, by bound, by weekday, or by name.

`barred`, not `disabled`: the calendar is a form control now, and
`HelixFormElement.disabled` is a boolean about the whole control. A method
and a flag cannot share a name, and of the two it is the method that should
move, because "disabled" on a control means one thing everywhere else in
the library.

members.name: show
members.description:
Moves the view, announcing it first.

`helix-navigate` and not `helix-change`: paging chooses nothing, and a
consumer driving the view has to hear that it moved without being told the
answer did. In controlled mode nothing moves and the consumer decides,
which is the point of them holding it.

members.name: select
members.description:
Adds a date to the selection, as the mode allows.

`range` starts over once it holds two, so a third click begins a new range
rather than extending or replacing an end at random. `multiple` toggles, so
clicking a chosen date takes it out.

members.name: report
members.description:
Reports the dates to the form, one entry each.

`FormData` rather than the comma-joined string the property holds, because
`mode="multiple"` is genuinely several answers and a server reading
`dates=2026-08-04,2026-08-06` has to know to split it on a convention this
library invented. One entry per date is what every other multi-valued
control on the platform sends, and `range` sends its two the same way, in
order, so start and end arrive as the pair they already are.

**Nothing at all without a `name`, and that is the mechanism rather than a
detail.** It is what lets a calendar sit inside something that owns the
form value, which is how `DatePicker` will hold one. The guard has to be
explicit here in a way it does not for `Listbox`: a control reporting a
plain string is skipped by the form when it has no name, but a `FormData`
carries its own names and its entries are appended whatever the element is
called, so an unnamed calendar would submit empty-named dates.

members.name: monthCount
members.description:
How many months are shown, clamped once.

`months` was clamped at the call site and read raw where the last month is
identified, so a zero, a negative or a non-numeric value rendered nothing
and took the forward control with it: `index === this.months - 1` is never
true for `NaN`. One getter both read.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: onValueChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the value is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. `onValueChange` and not `onChange`,
because React reserves the latter for its own synthetic system and wires
it to the native `change`, so a Helix event named `Change` would never
fire at all.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description: The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

has to remember to include it.

helix.documentation:
https://helix.fusion.dev/components/calendar

`helix-change` was `helix-select`, and it moved when the calendar became a
form control. A control whose value changes dispatches `helix-change` here:
`Input`, `Select`, `Listbox`, `Radio.Group` and `Toggle.Group` all do, and a
calendar submitting a date is the same kind of thing. `helix-select` stays
what it is elsewhere, which is a row or an item being chosen in something
that reports no value at all, such as `Menu` or `Tree`.

Paging is `helix-navigate` and not either of those, because it chooses
nothing: the view moves and the answer does not.

declarations.description:
`severity` lives on the headless tier rather than being an `appearance` on the
styled one, because it is meaning and not decoration. It picks the icon and
that icon's accessible name, so a reader who cannot see that the box is red
still hears "Error". A callout whose severity existed only as a color would
say nothing to them at all.

The icon is the fallback content of a slot, so a consumer replaces it by
slotting their own and the default disappears with no emptiness check. That
is what slot fallback is for.

Not an `Announcement`, which is the other thing this could be mistaken for.
A callout interrupts a document to set a passage apart and is read where it
sits; an announcement is page-level chrome above the masthead, announces
itself as a live region, and can be dismissed. Neither is a variant of the
other.

declarations.description:
Regions are slots rather than separate elements, because a header, body, and
footer carry no state, no behavior, and no API of their own. Slotting them
costs one custom element instead of five and lets the consumer bring their
own markup, so a title can be a real `<h2>` rather than an emulated one.

The host is the surface. A wrapper `<div part="container">` would be a second
box doing nothing the host cannot: the element itself takes the border, the
radius, and the grid, and a consumer styles `helix-card` rather than reaching
through `::part`. One node instead of two, on every card on the page.

Name the card with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`. That is the only
naming that survives server rendering: reading a title out of the light DOM
needs a DOM, and the server has none.

declarations.description:
The track is a scroller with scroll snapping, so a drag, a trackpad swipe,
and the browser's own momentum all work without being reimplemented. The
controls scroll it; they do not drive a transform.

Slides are the consumer's own elements. Each is given
`aria-roledescription="slide"` and a name reading its position in the set,
which is what a screen-reader user needs to know where they are. Where a
slide carries its own `aria-label`, that one is left alone.

**Rotation stops on focus and on hover, and once stopped it stays stopped.**
The APG is explicit: rotation must not resume unless the reader asks for it,
so hovering away does not start it again. The control names the action it
performs, and it is first in the tab order.

members.description:

script assigning to a native control does. Which mode the carousel is in is
read once, at the first update, from whether anything had declared an

announces where it would have gone; not declared, and the carousel owns it
and `default-index` says where it starts.

extracted, because a slide is addressed by position and every one of those
mixins is keyed by a name. One consumer is not a mixin: if a second numeric
state turns up, this is what it is extracted from.

members.description:

declarations.description:
The host is the group, so `role="group"` sits on it through internals and
`label` names it. A run of checkboxes with no name is announced as separate
controls, which is what the grouping exists to say it is not.

**Each checkbox still submits itself.** They are form-associated already and
a native group is several inputs sharing a name, so this adds no form value
of its own: it would submit the same answers twice. What it adds is the
grouping, a shared `name` so it is written once, and one place to read and
write the whole set.

`value` is the checked values, comma separated, in the order the boxes are
written. Setting it ticks exactly those and unticks the rest.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the whole set is out of play.

Its own property rather than an inherited one, because this group is not
form-associated and `disabled` arrives with `HelixFormElement`. The boxes
are each form-associated and have their own, which is exactly why the two
have to be reconciled rather than simply written over.

members.name: name
members.description: Name submitted with the form, given to every box that has none.

members.name: value
members.description: The checked values, comma separated.

members.name: boxes
members.description: The boxes, in light-DOM order. Client only: the server has no tree.

members.name: sync
members.description:
Pushes the group's name and value onto the boxes.

As properties rather than attributes. A `name` written onto a box is a
change to markup the consumer rendered, which a React consumer's hydration
reports and does not patch up. A box that names itself keeps its own.

members.name: seed
members.description:
Reads the boxes' own state into `value`, once, before anything is pushed.

`sync` used to refuse to write anything while `value` was empty, and the
guard was there for this: a group written with no `value` and boxes that
declare their own `checked` would have had them all cleared on the first
update. What it also did was make `group.value = ''` do nothing at all, so
the obvious way to clear a group silently did not, and the last box could
not be unticked through the group either.

Seeding is the honest version of the same intent. The markup decides the
starting set, exactly as before, and from then on `value` is what the boxes
follow, including when it is empty. The group's `value` is a derived read
of the boxes rather than state it owns, so reading it out of them at the
start is what it already means.

members.name: handleChange
members.description:
Reads a box's requested change into `value`, and says so once.

The box is found from the event's target, which does two things. It tells
the group which box asked, where the detail carries only the shared name.
And it ignores the group's own dispatch, which lands on this same listener
because the group is what it is dispatched from: without the guard the
group answers itself until the stack gives out.

The requested state comes from the event rather than from the box. Driving
the boxes from `value` makes them controlled, so a controlled box applies
nothing on its own and reports what it was asked for. Reading `checked`
here would read the state it still holds and nothing would ever change.

members.name: validate
members.description:
Refuses an empty set where one was required, which nothing did.

`required` arrives with `MixinField`, reflects, and paints the asterisk
through the composed field sheet, and enforced nothing at all: no validity,
no message, and nothing cascading to the boxes. A group marked required
submitted empty.

The group is deliberately not form-associated, its boxes being the controls,
so the validity is reported through the group's own internals and anchored
on the list: the browser needs somewhere to point the message.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

has to remember to include it.

are each form-associated and have their own, which is exactly why the two
have to be reconciled rather than simply written over.

declarations.summary: Groups related checkboxes, and reports them as one set.

helix.documentation:
https://helix.fusion.dev/components/checkbox-group

**Its message is always given, never derived.** Every form-related member of
`ElementInternals` throws on an element that is not form-associated, and this
one is not, on purpose: the boxes submit themselves. So `feedback` is what
shows here, and the browser has nothing to say about a set it does not know
is a set.

declarations.description:
Renders a real `<input type="checkbox">`, so the space key, the focus ring,
and the indeterminate glyph come from the platform. `delegatesFocus` puts
focus on it, and it serializes into the server's markup, so the control is
reachable before any script loads.

**The input inside a shadow root submits nothing**, because the form is on
the other side of the boundary. The host is form-associated instead and
reports its own value through `ElementInternals`, which is also what carries
validity and what answers a form reset.

A checked box submits its `value`, and an unchecked one submits nothing at
all. That is what a native checkbox does, and a form built around one reads
the absence rather than a `false`.

`indeterminate` is presentation and nothing else. It is neither checked nor
unchecked to a reader, it never submits, and the first click resolves it: a
third state that survives interaction is a control nobody can finish.

members.name: handleLabelChange
members.description:
Whether there is a label to leave room for, written to the host.

The row is a flex line with a gap in it, so a label span rendered empty is
still a box and still takes that gap: an unlabelled box came out with eight
pixels of nothing after it. The input answers this by not rendering the
element, which cannot work here, because a checkbox is named by its own
content and the property is only that slot's fallback. Gating on the
property would unlabel every `<helix-checkbox>Text</helix-checkbox>` ever
written.

So the slot is asked instead, the same way `Tooltip` asks its own: with
`flatten`, because here the fallback counts, being where the property
renders. Client only, so a server-rendered unlabelled checkbox carries the
gap for one frame. That is a control with no accessible name, which has a
worse problem than its spacing.

members.name: syncLabelPresence
members.description:
Asks the slot, and says the answer on the host.

Called on `slotchange` and after every update, and the second is not
belt-and-braces: **`slotchange` does not fire when nothing is assigned.**
So a checkbox labelled only by its property, which is most of them, never
heard about its own label and rendered without one. Caught by the spec that
asks a labelled row to be wider than a bare one.

members.name: checked
members.description:
Whether the control is checked.

One property rather than two. Reading gives the real state whichever
mode the control is in; writing hands ownership to the consumer, which
is what the attribute in `<helix-checkbox checked>` does as well. The
same shape all four of these mixins have, for the reason given on
`MixinControllerOpen.open`.

Not reflected: the attribute is the consumer's input and stays as they
wrote it, and `data-checked` carries the resolved state for stylesheets.

members.name: defaultChecked
members.description: Initial checked state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: checkedState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: checkedMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `checked` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: onCheckedChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the state is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. And not reachable from React's JSX,
which reserves every `on[A-Z]` prop for its own event system and drops
what it does not recognize; the generated wrapper listens for the event
instead.

members.name: requestChecked
members.description:
Requests a checked change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the
`helix-change` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode
the element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing
and waits for the consumer to pass a new `checked`, which is what
"controlled" means.

members.name: toggleChecked
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: resetChecked
members.description:
Drops the uncontrolled state, so the control reads `defaultChecked`
again.

A form reset has to return a control to what its markup declared, and
clearing `checked` alone only leaves controlled mode. The value the
element has been keeping lives here, so this is where it is dropped.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled

Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two

renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name

there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

declarations.summary: A box that is ticked, or not, or neither.

declarations.description:
A real `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`, not a div with a role and a
hand-built trap. The platform gives four things that are each a day's work to
reimplement and easy to get subtly wrong: the top layer, so the dialog is
above everything regardless of what `z-index` anyone else wrote; a real
backdrop; Escape; and inert-behind, so the page underneath is not reachable
by pointer, keyboard, or a screen reader's virtual cursor.

**`open` drives `showModal()`, and every way it can close comes back through
`requestOpen`.** A native dialog can close from three directions: the
property, Escape, and a `<form method="dialog">` submit inside it. Left
alone, two of those would shut the dialog while the consumer's state still
said open, which is the bug that makes a modal impossible to reopen. Escape
is intercepted and routed through the request, so `preventDefault()` on the
`helix-close` refuses it; a close that happens anyway is reflected back.

**Nothing here traps focus.** `showModal()` does it, and better: `inert` on
the rest of the document is something no JavaScript trap can achieve.
`FocusTrapController` stays for the surfaces that are not modal.

The regions are bare slots rather than wrappers, for the reason the card's
are: an unassigned `<slot>` is `display: contents` and generates no box, so a
dialog with no footer has no empty band where one would be.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the dialog.

members.name: persistent
members.description:
Whether Escape and the backdrop can close it.

Off for a dialog that must be answered. It does not disable the close
control a consumer slots in: refusing to be dismissed is not the same as
refusing to be closed, and a dialog with no way out at all is a trap.

members.name: commands
members.default: new CommandController(this, { commands: { '--close': () => this.close(), '--show': () => this.show(), '--toggle': () => this.toggleOpen(), }, })

members.name: dialog
members.description: The native dialog, or nothing where there is no DOM to hold one.

members.name: show
members.description: Moves focus into the dialog and makes the rest of the page inert.

members.name: close
members.description: Asks to close, which a consumer may refuse.

members.name: handleCancel
members.description:
Escape, intercepted so it is a request rather than an act.

The native `cancel` event fires before the dialog closes, so preventing it
leaves the dialog open and lets `requestOpen` decide. Without this a reader
pressing Escape would close a dialog its consumer had said was open, and
the two would disagree until something else moved.

members.name: handleClose
members.description:
A close that happened anyway, reflected back.

`<form method="dialog">` closes the dialog directly and there is no event
to prevent. Rather than fight it, the state follows: the dialog is shut, so
saying otherwise would be a lie the next `showModal()` would trip over.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: onOpenChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the state is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. And not reachable from React's JSX,
which reserves every `on[A-Z]` prop for its own event system and drops
what it does not recognize; the generated wrapper listens for the events
instead.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on

makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what

members.description:

Off by default, and out of the accessibility tree. Most rules on a page
separate nothing: they underline a heading or close a section that space

screen-reader user has to walk past.

declarations.description:
A row that opens a page *contains* that page: its rows are this row's own
children, assigned to the `page` slot. The tree is the structure, so there
are no ids to wire and a consumer who moves a row has moved its page with it.

**It renders one of three things**, and which one is the stack's business
rather than its own. On the page showing, it is a row. Showing its own page,
it contributes that page's rows and nothing else, because its row belongs to
the page above. On neither, it renders nothing at all: the rows are in the
light DOM and come back untouched, so there is no state to keep and nothing
to hide with an attribute this element would have to write onto itself.

Choosing is announced, never applied. The row dispatches and the stack
decides whether that means drilling in or choosing a command.

declarations.description:
One panel that changes rather than panels opening beside each other. That is
the right shape wherever there is no room for a second column: a phone has
none, and a touch screen has no hover to open one with.

**Not a `Menu`, and the difference is what it is for rather than how it
looks.** A menu is a thing that opens from a trigger and closes when it is
done; this is a region that sits where it is put, inside a drawer or a
sidebar or a settings panel. `Menu` drills too, through the same controller,
because a menu deep enough to need pages wants exactly this behavior without
being this component.

**Navigation, never a value.** Rows are places to go and commands to run, so
nothing here is form-associated and nothing is submitted. A drill-down that
reported a value would be a `Listbox` whose options happen to nest, and that
is the component to reach for instead.

**The tree is the state.** A row that opens a page contains that page, so the
stack holds one reference and reads the rest from the DOM. See
`DrilldownController`, which is where this behavior lives and which `Menu`
shares.

declarations.description:
An empty region with no explanation is indistinguishable from one that failed
to load, so this exists to tell the difference: what would be here, and the
one action that would put something here.

`role="status"` on a polite live region, because an empty view usually
arrives in place of content that was being fetched. Announcing it is the only
way a screen-reader user learns the search returned nothing, rather than
being left waiting.

Every region is a bare slot. The reference ships an `empty-state-heading` and
an `empty-state-actions` whose only job is to assign themselves a slot on
connect, which is a component for something the consumer can write.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.description:
Everything a button does, with one thing added and it is the reason this is
an element rather than a note on `Button`: **an icon-only control has no
accessible name unless it is given one.** A button whose content is a glyph
announces as "button" and nothing else, which is the single most common way a
toolbar becomes unusable without sight. `label` is not optional in practice,
and having a component that says so is what makes it reviewable.

**Registered, so it can be rendered and not only subclassed.** The styled
icon button extended `HelixBaseButton` directly, which left no
`helix-base-icon-button` for anything to use: a headless consumer wanting an
icon button had a button and a naming convention. Anything in this tier that
needs one, such as an announcement's dismiss control, can now render it
without reaching into the styled tier for a tag that would never upgrade.

Top-level rather than `Button.Icon`, because a namespace means composition
and an icon-only button is not part of a button. It is a button with
different content and a different shape, which makes it its own component.

attributes.name: command
attributes.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

attributes.name: commandfor
attributes.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

attributes.name: disabled
attributes.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

attributes.name: name
attributes.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: commandFor
members.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Moves focus to the inner control, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: focusable
members.description:
Whether the button holds its group's tab stop.

A toolbar keeps one tab stop across its children, and the obvious way to do
that is to write `tabindex` onto each of them. That is a change to markup
the consumer rendered, so a React consumer's hydration reports it and does
not patch it up. A parent sets this property instead, which writes nothing,
and the stop lands on the inner control inside the shadow root.

No attribute, because it is coordination between elements rather than
anything a consumer sets.

members.name: linkCommand
members.description:
Points the inner button at the command's target, by reference.

**The attribute cannot do this and it fails silently.** `commandfor` is an
IDREF, and an IDREF resolves inside the tree it is written in: forwarded
onto a button in this shadow root it looks for the id *here*, finds
nothing, and the trigger does nothing at all. Measured before this existed:
the button clicked, no `command` event was dispatched, and there was
nothing anywhere to say why.

`commandForElement` takes an element instead, and an element reference
resolves outward: a node in a shadow root may point at one in the document.
The same asymmetry the listbox relies on for `aria-activedescendant`, and
the second place in this library where the id form is the one that cannot
work.

The id is looked up in the host's own root rather than the document, so a
button inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root
and not a coincidence in the page.

members.name: commandTarget
members.description:
The element this button commands, or nothing.

Looked up in the button's own root rather than in the document, so a button
inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root and not
a coincidence in the page.

members.name: sendCommand
members.description:
Sends the `command` event where the browser will not.

Invoker commands are recent, and where they are missing `linkCommand` set a
property that does not exist and returned, so the button did nothing at all
when clicked. Silently: the markup was right, the component was right, and
every `command` in the library was inert at once with no error to find. A
design system cannot ship an example that depends on a feature failing that
quietly.

Only where the platform is absent, so a browser that has invokers sends
exactly one event and this sends none. Doing both would open a dialog and
immediately toggle it shut again, which is a worse bug than the one this
fixes and would only appear on the browsers that work.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

declarations.description:
The set is Phosphor, drawn on a 256 box at stroke-width 16, and each glyph is
rendered as its own inner markup rather than as a single path. Most icons are
several elements at once, each with its own stroke and fill, so a one-path
model would draw a fraction of the set and quietly drop the rest.

**The markup is trusted by construction.** It is generated at build time from
SVG files in this repository, never from anything a user supplies, which is
what makes `unsafeSVG` the right tool rather than a risk.

The `<svg>` carries `fill="currentColor"` because the generator keeps only
the inner markup and discards the source's own root tag, and that tag is
where Phosphor puts its fill. Without it, every solid glyph in the set, 65 of
them, falls back to the SVG default of black and disappears on a dark page.
Shapes that set their own `fill` or `stroke` are unaffected, which is why the
outline icons looked fine and hid this.

A name with no match renders nothing at all instead of an empty box, so a
typo cannot leave a hole in a layout that looks deliberate.

An icon is decorative by default and hidden from assistive technology. Give
it a `label` only when the icon is the sole carrier of meaning, such as
inside a button with no text.

declarations.description:
Renders a real `<input>`, so the caret, selection, autofill, spellcheck, the
password manager, and the on-screen keyboard a phone chooses all come from the
platform. `delegatesFocus` puts focus on it, and it serializes into the
server's markup, so the field is usable before any script loads.

**The input inside a shadow root submits nothing**, because the form is on the
other side of the boundary. The host is form-associated instead and reports
its own value through `ElementInternals`, which is also what carries validity
and what answers a form reset.

`value` and `defaultValue` are separate for the reason `checked` and
`defaultChecked` are: `value` is what is in the field now and
`defaultValue` is what the markup asked for, which is where a reset returns
to and is gone the moment anyone types.

**Validity is the platform's.** The `type` and `required` are set on the real
input and its `validity` is copied onto the host, so an email field rejects
what the browser says is not an email rather than what a regular expression
here guesses. What this adds is the anchor, so `reportValidity` points the
bubble at the input rather than at the host.

`pattern`, `minlength` and `maxlength` are **not** forwarded, and this
paragraph used to say they were, on the strength of "and the rest": no such
properties exist and nothing binds them, so a consumer following the sentence
wrote an attribute on the host that reached no input and constrained nothing.
They are worth adding and are a change to the API rather than a correction to
a comment, so what is here is the truth about what is forwarded today.
