members.name: placeholder
members.description: Shown while the field is empty. Not a label: it goes when typing starts.

members.name: readOnly
members.description: Whether the field refuses input while still submitting its value.

members.name: type
members.description: What the field accepts, which decides the keyboard and the validation.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Focus is delegated to the input, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: handleInput
members.description:
Every keystroke, cancelable, and put back where it is refused.

The input has already taken the character by the time this runs, so a
consumer that refuses the change has to see the field returned to what the
element still holds. Otherwise the text on screen and the value the form
would submit disagree, which is the one thing a controlled field must never
do.

members.name: handleChange
members.description: Relayed, because `change` does not cross a shadow boundary on its own.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the value and the validity the host stands behind.

members.name: focus
members.description: Puts the caret in the field, the way a label pointing at one would.

members.name: select
members.description: Selects everything in the field.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: onValueChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the value is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. `onValueChange` and not `onChange`,
because React reserves the latter for its own synthetic system and wires
it to the native `change`, so a Helix event named `Change` would never
fire at all.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

members.name: name
members.description:

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: kind
members.description:
What kind of list this is, which is a fact about the content.

On the headless tier because it is meaning rather than decoration, the same
argument `severity` makes on `Callout`. A numbered list is numbered because
the order carries information; a bulleted one is bulleted because the items
are a set and the order does not. That distinction is the reader's, and it
has to survive with the stylesheet turned off.

- `default` is a run of rows and takes no marker. It is what a list of
  settings or files is: neither ordered nor a set to be counted.
- `ordered` numbers them, for steps.
- `unordered` bullets them, for a set.
- `description` pairs each row's label with its supporting text as a term
  and what the term means.

**`description` reuses the row's existing slots rather than inventing a
  second kind of row.** A term and its description is exactly the label and
  the supporting text `List.Item` already has, so the kind changes how the
  pair is drawn and nothing about what a consumer writes. A separate
  `List.Term` element would be a second row shape for one attribute's sake.

declarations.summary: A set of rows, read as a set.

declarations.description:
**The listbox is the control and the options are its vocabulary.** A Select
is this with a trigger in front of it, a Combobox is this with a text input,
and a command palette is this again: they differ in what opens the list and
what filters it, not in what the list is. Building it as its own family is
what stops each of those reimplementing the keyboard and the filtering.

**`value` is comma separated when `multiple` is set**, the way
`Checkbox.Group`'s is. It stays a string because that is what a form submits
and what `MixinControllerValue` holds; an array property would be a second
shape for the same fact, and the two would disagree the first time one was
set without the other.

**Chosen and active are two different things.** Chosen is the answer; active
is where the keyboard is. In a single-select list they move together, which
is the radio group pattern and is what a reader expects from arrow keys. With
`multiple` they come apart: the arrows move without choosing and Space
chooses, because a reader passing over four options on the way to the fifth
did not mean to pick all five.

That is also why this does not use `KeyboardNavigationController`, which
moves and chooses in one act by design. Half of this component needs that and
half needs the opposite, and a flag on the controller would be this paragraph
written twice.

**Filtering hides rather than removes.** An option the filter has hidden is
still the consumer's element in the consumer's order, so a filter that clears
puts the list back exactly as it was with nothing re-rendered. What counts as
a match is a plain case-insensitive substring, and a consumer wanting more
hides options itself: `filter` is a convenience over the same `hidden` the
component uses.
declarations.name: HelixBaseListbox

cssParts.description: Shown when a filter has hidden everything.
cssParts.name: empty

cssParts.description: The region holding the field that narrows the list.
cssParts.name: search

slots.description: The options, and any groups of them.

members.name: filter
members.description:
What the list is narrowed to, if anything.

Filtering hides rather than removes, so nothing about the value changes and
the list is still the consumer's own elements in their own order. Reading
gives what is being filtered on; writing declares it theirs, and
`default-filter` seeds one the list owns.

members.name: defaultFilter
members.description: What to start narrowed to, where nothing declared it.

members.name: filterState
members.description: What the list is narrowed to, whoever set it.

members.name: filterMode
members.description: Whether the consumer owns the narrowing, decided once and then fixed.

members.name: filterable
members.description:
Whether the list renders a field for narrowing itself.

The field lives here rather than in whatever frames the list, because the
filtering already does: `filter`, the empty state and the keyboard are all
this component's. A select that drew its own search box above a listbox
would be writing the same field again, and so would a combobox, and so
would a command palette, which is the fault the three-family split exists
to prevent.

members.name: filterLabel
members.description: Placeholder for the field that narrows the list.

members.name: multiple
members.description: Whether more than one option can be the answer.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: What is shown when a filter has hidden every option.

members.name: activeValue
members.description: Which option the keyboard is on, which is not what is chosen.

members.name: hasMatches
members.description:
Whether anything survived the filter, kept as state rather than counted at
render time.

Counting during render reads the hiding from the *previous* pass, because
hiding happens in `updated` against options that are the consumer's
elements rather than this component's markup. So a filter matching nothing
rendered the full list, hid every option, and left an empty box with no
message in it: the count was right one pass too late. Written to state
instead, which schedules the one further render that shows it.

members.name: options
members.description:
Every option, in the order a reader meets them.

Descendants rather than children, because a group puts a level between the
list and its options and the keyboard has to move through a grouped list
exactly as it moves through a flat one.

members.name: collect
members.description:
Walks the tree, and walks *through* a slot when it meets one.

Descendants rather than children, because a group puts a level between the
list and its options and the keyboard has to move through a grouped list
exactly as it moves through a flat one.

Through a slot because that is how this gets composed. `Select` renders a
listbox in its own shadow root with a slot inside it, so the options are
the *select's* light DOM and the listbox's only child is the slot: a plain
`querySelectorAll` finds the slot and no options at all, and the whole
component comes up empty. Found the first time the two were put together,
which is the argument for building the pieces separately rather than
discovering it inside a finished Select.

members.name: groups
members.description: The groups, found the same way and for the same reason.

members.name: shown
members.description: The options a filter has left showing.

members.name: values
members.description: The chosen values, which is a list whether or not `multiple` is set.

members.name: choose
members.description:
Applies a choice, announcing first so a listener can refuse it.

With `multiple` a choice is a toggle, because the same press has to be able
to take an answer back; without it a choice replaces whatever was there.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
Moves the keyboard, and chooses with it only where that is the pattern.

Space and Enter are how a multi-select list chooses, and they are also how
a single-select one confirms what the arrows already did, so they act
either way rather than being guarded on `multiple`.

members.name: place
members.description: Hides what the filter excludes, and writes the rest onto the options.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the answer and the verdict on it.

members.name: linkActive
members.description:
Points the focused list at the option the keyboard is on.

**The gap this closes.** Focus stays on `[part="items"]` while a highlight
moves between options, which is the half of the ARIA listbox pattern we
had. The other half is saying *which* option, and nothing did: a screen
reader heard the list and its selection and never heard the item being
moved over. Neither `aria-activedescendant` nor a roving `tabindex` was
wired, and the pattern requires one of the two.

**An element reference and not an id, because an IDREF cannot do this.**
The options are the consumer's light DOM and the element that takes focus
is in this shadow root, so `aria-activedescendant="whatever"` resolves
against the shadow tree, finds nothing, and is dropped in silence. Element
references are the platform's answer to exactly that, and they resolve
outward: a shadow-tree element may point at a light-DOM one, which is the
direction this needs.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, for the reason `hostAria` gives:
assigning to a property an engine does not implement is a no-op rather than
an error, so the guard is what makes the absence visible to anyone reading
this. Where it is missing the list still works and still announces its
selection; what is lost is the running commentary as the keys move.

members.name: handleFilter
members.description:
Narrows the list as the reader types, announcing it first.

`helix-filter` and not `helix-change`, because nothing about the value
changes: the options are hidden rather than removed, and telling a consumer
their answer moved when it did not is worse than telling them nothing. It
told them nothing before this.

members.name: requestFilter
members.description: Requests a narrowing, and reports whether the request stood.

members.name: handleFilterKeydown
members.description:
Sends the keys that belong to the list to the list.

A reader filtering is still choosing: they type two letters and press Down
to reach what is left, and the field would otherwise swallow it because the
arrows move a caret. Typing keys stay with the field, which is what makes
this different from forwarding everything.

Escape clears rather than closing. What frames the list may close on Escape
too, so this stops the event when there is something to clear: one press
empties the filter, a second reaches whatever is above and closes it. A
filter that closed the panel would lose the reader's place for a keystroke
they meant as an undo.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description:
Focusing the host focuses the list inside it.

The focusable node is `[part="items"]`, a div in this shadow root, and a
caller outside has no way to reach it: `select` opened its panel and called
`.focus()` on this element, which is not focusable, so focus stayed on the
trigger and the arrow keys never reached the options at all. Delegation is
the platform answering that, and it keeps `document.activeElement` on the
host, which is what a caller reasons about.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: onValueChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the value is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. `onValueChange` and not `onChange`,
because React reserves the latter for its own synthetic system and wires
it to the native `change`, so a Helix event named `Change` would never
fire at all.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.description:
Three shapes, one element, because a reader moving down a menu with the
arrow keys does not care which kind each row is and neither should the
markup. What it is follows from what it was given: something slotted into
`submenu` makes it a way in, `checked` makes it a choice, and neither makes
it a command.

**The role follows the shape.** A row that can be ticked is
`menuitemcheckbox` and carries `aria-checked`, because a reader is told "one
of these is on" rather than "here is a button". A row that opens a page keeps
`menuitem` and says `aria-haspopup`, since the page it opens is a menu.

Whether it is on the page showing is set by the menu as a property, never as
an attribute: an attribute written onto a consumer's element after it
upgrades is a hydration mismatch waiting to happen.

documented. Lit's element shim carries attributes but not a tree, so

reader on the strength of a guess.

declarations.description:
The trigger is slotted and stays the consumer's own element, the same way the
tooltip takes one. The surface is rendered here, in the top layer through the
popover API, so it clears any ancestor with `overflow: hidden` without a
`z-index` anywhere.

**It drills down rather than flying out.** A submenu replaces what is on
screen and a back row returns, instead of opening a second panel beside the
first. Panels beside panels need a diagonal path a pointer has to travel
without straying, they run off the edge of a narrow window, and on a touch
screen there is no hover to open them with at all. One panel that changes
what it holds has none of those problems and reads the same on a phone.

The open page is held here rather than in each item, because only one page
shows at a time and something has to know which. Items are told by property,
not by attribute: an attribute written onto a consumer's element after it
upgrades is a hydration mismatch waiting to happen.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: onOpenChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the state is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. And not reachable from React's JSX,
which reserves every `on[A-Z]` prop for its own event system and drops
what it does not recognize; the generated wrapper listens for the events
instead.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

a header is not inherently navigation, and navigation is not only ever in a
header: a footer and a sidebar hold the same thing.

reason it is a component. A marker that moves needs something that knows
where every item is, and reading `aria-current` is how it knows which: the
thing that makes the page announce correctly is the same thing that puts the
marker in the right place.

declarations.description:
**Its own family rather than a part of Select, and the reason is what it
belongs to.** `role="option"` requires an owning `role="listbox"`, which is
the ARIA contract: an option cannot stand alone. But a Select is *a listbox
with a trigger*, a Combobox is *a listbox with a text input*, and a command
palette is the same listbox again. The thing an option belongs to is the
listbox, not any one control that happens to contain one.

That is the difference from `Radio`, which is a part of its group: a radio
has exactly one kind of owner, and an option has several.

Selection is announced rather than applied, the way a radio's is. The option
says it was chosen, the listbox decides whether that stands, and the listbox
writes `selected` back. An option that selected itself would be a second
answer to which one is chosen.

**Nothing here knows about filtering.** A hidden option is hidden by whatever
owns it, through `hidden`, because what counts as a match is the listbox's
question and differs between a select and a command palette.

declarations.description:
A table of contents, named for the job. Three of the obvious names are taken
by things that are not this: `Outline` is a CSS property and the focus ring's
whole vocabulary, `Contents` is `display: contents` and the `content` part
half this library renders, and `TableOfContents` would sit beside `Table` and
`TableColumn` and read as a third part of that family. `PageNav` sits beside
`NavBar`, which is the same job at the other scale: one navigates a site, the
other navigates a document.

**The links are the consumer's own anchors**, the same as `NavBar`. A router
renders its own `<a>` and cannot render one inside this shadow root, and the
hrefs are fragments the page already knows.

**What is current is decided by position, not by intersection.** The obvious
build is an `IntersectionObserver` with a thin band near the top of the
window, and it fails in both directions: with headings far apart nothing is
in the band and the marker goes out entirely, and with headings close
together several are and it flickers between them. So the observer is only
the *trigger*, and the answer is computed from where the headings actually
are: the current section is the last one whose top has passed the reading
line, or the first heading before any of them has.

That rule is what a reader means. Two headings on screen at once are not
ambiguous to a person: they are reading under the upper one.

**`aria-current="location"`, and it is written onto the consumer's anchor.**
This library does not normally write to light-DOM children, because an
attribute added after upgrade is one a server's markup never had. It is right
here for the reason `Carousel` names its slides: what is current is derived
from scroll position, so no server could have rendered it and there is
nothing for hydration to disagree with. `location` rather than `page`, which
is what `NavBar` uses: `page` means this is the page, and every one of these
is the same page.

declarations.description:
The general case the specific overlays are versions of. `Menu` holds
commands, `Select` holds options, `Tooltip` holds a description; this holds
whatever the consumer puts in it, which is why it has no keyboard of its own
and no opinion about what is inside.

**The trigger is slotted and stays the consumer's own element.** Nothing is
written onto it: no `aria-expanded`, no `id`, no `tabindex`. A component that
decorates a consumer's markup after upgrading is a component whose output a
React consumer's hydration disagrees with, and the attribute they would care
about most is the one that changes on every open.

**The panel is in the top layer**, through the popover API, so it clears any
ancestor with `overflow: hidden` without a `z-index` fight. `position: fixed`
does not do that: it is still clipped by `overflow`, and re-anchored entirely
by an ancestor carrying `transform`, `filter` or `contain`.

**It opens on click, and from a command.** `command="--show"` and its
siblings work here the way they do on `Dialog` and `Drawer`, so a trigger
elsewhere on the page can open it without a line of script and without being
slotted into it.

members.default: new PopoverController(this, { anchor: () => this.trigger, /* The host, not the panel. `display: contents` leaves it without a box, so a press on the trigger is inside the host and outside the panel, and a boundary of the panel alone would close on the very press that opened it. */ /* The host *and* whatever invoked it. An outside press is measured against this, and a `--toggle` button outside the host is part of the control by any reading a reader would give it: pressing it while the panel is open should close it once, not close it on `pointerdown` and reopen it on the `click` that follows. */ boundary: (): (HTMLElement | undefined)[] => [this, this.invoker], offset: () => this.offset, onDismiss: () => this.hide(), placement: () => this.placement, surface: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="popover"]'), })

members.name: invoker
members.description:
The invoker that last opened the panel, when a command did.

The handlers discarded the `source` the controller hands them, which cost
two things at once. The panel was positioned against the host, and the
styled tier makes the host a boxless `display: contents` element, so a
popover opened by a command outside it opened against the window origin.
And the outside-press dismissal had no way to know the invoker was part of
the control: the press fires on `pointerdown`, the command arrives on the
`click` after it, so a `--toggle` button outside the host closed the panel
and immediately reopened it, for ever.

members.description: Closes the panel and puts focus back on the trigger.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: onOpenChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the state is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. And not reachable from React's JSX,
which reserves every `on[A-Z]` prop for its own event system and drops
what it does not recognize; the generated wrapper listens for the events
instead.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

declarations.description:
Determinate by default, and `indeterminate` for a task whose total is not
known yet. `Spinner` is still the right answer where the wait is short or has
no place of its own on the page; a bar earns its width where the work is the
subject of the region it sits in.

A bar that fills at a made-up rate would be a bar that lies, so the
indeterminate one does not fill: it runs a segment across the track, which
says work is happening and claims no proportion at all. `aria-valuenow` is
omitted with it, which is the platform's own signal for the same thing.

**The fill is a percentage of the track, written as a custom property.** It
is derived from `value` and `max` rather than measured, so it renders on a
server with no layout and needs nothing after upgrade. That is what keeps it
out of the class of geometry this library writes only on the client.

**`value` is clamped, and out-of-range input is not an error.** A count that
runs past its own total is ordinary in real applications, and a bar that
overflows its track or reports `aria-valuenow` above `aria-valuemax` is worse
than one that reads as finished.

Semantics are on the host through `ElementInternals`, the same as everywhere
else: a `role` in the shadow root announces correctly and leaves the host
anonymous to anything walking the light DOM, and a `role` written onto the
host as an attribute is one a server's markup never had.

nothing. `value` and `max` are ignored while it is set.

page is busy; a bar says a named piece of work is running, and keeps its
place in the layout when the answer arrives and it becomes determinate.

Renders a real `<q>`, which is what supplies the quotation marks: the browser
inserts the right ones for the document's language, and nests them correctly
when one quotation sits inside another. Typing the marks into the content
instead gets both of those wrong in every language but one.

A passage set off from the prose rather than run inside it is a blockquote,
which is a different element for a different job.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.description: URL identifying where the quotation came from.

declarations.summary: A short quotation, set inline with the text around it.

declarations.description:
**The group is the control, and the radios are its options.** This is the
asymmetry with checkboxes and it comes from what a form submits: a set of
checkboxes is several answers and each box submits its own, while a set of
radios is one answer, so the group owns the `name`, the `value` and the
validity, and a lone radio outside a group is not a control at all.

Which is also why `MixinField` lands here and not on `Radio`: the label, the
hint and the message are about the question, and the question is the set.

Selection travels up and state travels down. An item announces that it was
chosen, the group decides whether that stands, and the group writes
`selected` onto every item. Nothing sets itself, so there is one answer to
"which one is on" rather than one per item.

`value` and `defaultValue` are separate for the reason `checked` and
`defaultChecked` are: `value` is the answer now, `defaultValue` is what the
markup asked for, which is where a reset returns and is gone the moment
anything is chosen.

members.name: handleSelection
members.description:
Announces before it applies, so a listener can refuse the change.

The item has not moved by the time this runs, unlike a native input, so
refusing is simply not writing the value: there is nothing to put back.

members.name: place
members.description: Writes the answer onto the items, and nothing onto the host.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the answer and the verdict on it.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: onValueChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the value is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. `onValueChange` and not `onChange`,
because React reserves the latter for its own synthetic system and wires
it to the native `change`, so a Helix event named `Change` would never
fire at all.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description: The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

declarations.description:
Renders a `<button role="radio">`, not an `<input type="radio">`, and the
reason is the shadow boundary rather than preference: native radios group by
sharing a `name` within a form, and a radio inside a shadow root cannot join
a group on the other side of it. The group is the form control here, so the
option only has to say what it is and announce when it is chosen.

**It carries no label of its own.** A radio is named by the words beside it,
which is its own content, and the label, hint and message of the *set* belong
to the group. This is the one control in the family that takes nothing from
`MixinField`, because a lone radio is not a control: it is an answer to one.

Selection is announced rather than applied. The item dispatches, the group
decides, and the group writes `selected` back. An item that set itself would
be a second source of truth for which one is on.

declarations.description:
**A trigger and a `Listbox`, not a listbox reimplemented behind a button.**
The list this opens is the same element a consumer can use on its own, with
the same keyboard, the same filtering and the same multi-select rules. What
Select adds is the closing: a trigger that says what is chosen, a surface
that floats, and somewhere for focus to go back to.

The options are the consumer's, in the consumer's light DOM, slotted through
into the listbox. That is why the listbox walks through slots to find them:
from its point of view the options belong to something else.

**What it does not do is duplicate the value.** `Select` owns it, hands it
down, and takes changes back; the listbox is the thing being operated and not
a second place the answer lives.

members.name: filterable
members.description:
Whether the list can be narrowed by typing.

Passed to the listbox rather than acted on here, because the listbox owns
the filtering, the empty state and the keyboard. This property existed and
was never read: it reflected, it type-checked, and nothing anywhere
rendered a field. API that does nothing is worse than API that is missing,
because a consumer sets it and believes it.

members.description: Whether more than one option can be the answer.

members.name: placeholder
members.description: Shown on the trigger while nothing is chosen.

members.name: listbox
members.description:
The list inside the surface, or nothing where there is no DOM to hold one.

The optional chain is the server. `renderRoot` is a property Lit's element
shim does not carry, and this getter is reached from `display`, which is
read during `render`: without it the select threw on every server render
and could not be served at all. Found by writing its SSR spec, which is
the only thing that would have found it, because the client is where every
other path runs and the client always has a root.

The other reads of `renderRoot` here are inside callbacks the controllers
invoke, and a controller only runs on a connected element, so they cannot
be reached from the server and are left plain.

members.description: Closes the list and puts focus back where it came from.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: onOpenChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the state is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. And not reachable from React's JSX,
which reserves every `on[A-Z]` prop for its own event system and drops
what it does not recognize; the generated wrapper listens for the events
instead.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: valueMode

members.name: onValueChange

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.

editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on

submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: disabled

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
