members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback

members.name: name
members.description:

on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.summary: Stands in for content that has not arrived.

declarations.description:
A real `<input type="range">`, so the drag, the arrow keys, Home and End, the
page keys and the touch target are all the platform's. Every one of those is
a thing a hand-built slider gets wrong, and the last is the one nobody
notices: a native range has a hit area larger than its thumb, sized by the
platform for a finger.

**The value is a string, like every other form control's.** A range submits
text and `MixinControllerValue` holds text, so the number is a reading of the
value rather than the value itself. `valueAsNumber` is there for anything
doing arithmetic on it.

**Marks are drawn rather than left to `<datalist>`**, which was the first
answer and is the wrong one. A datalist's ticks cannot be styled at all, and
Firefox does not render them for a range at all, so the platform's version is
a mark that looks like someone else's design where it appears and no mark
where it does not. Drawing them costs the semantics nothing, because a mark
is decoration: what a reader can actually land on is `step`, which the input
enforces whether or not anything is drawn.

`markers` is a count rather than a flag tied to `step`. A flag reads well
until a slider from zero to a hundred stepping by one asks for a hundred and
one ticks, and then it is either noise or a silent refusal to draw. A number
is what the reader sees, so it cannot surprise anyone.

members.name: markers
members.description:
How many marks to draw along the track, evenly spaced, ends included.

`0` or `1` draws none: one mark on a track says nothing about a range.
They are decoration, so they are `aria-hidden`; what a reader can land on
is `step`, which the input enforces regardless.

**Each one is snapped to a step before it is placed.** Evenly spaced and
on a step are two different things, and asking for four marks across a
hundred in twenty-fives wants them at 0, 33.3, 66.7 and 100: two of those
are places the thumb cannot go. A mark the thumb can never sit on is the
one thing a mark must not be, so the spacing gives way rather than the
step, and marks may come out unevenly spaced when the two disagree. That
is the honest picture of the range being offered.

written in the markup ever worked, and the property that is the documented
API silently did not.

attribute the server's markup does not have and one that selector would
match, drawing the layout for no marks. So the boolean fact is mirrored to
a `data-` name, which is the rule this library already follows for state:
the stylesheet wants to know whether there are marks, not how many. How
many is what `markerValues` answers, and `< 2` is where it already draws
the line.

small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message

hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: formDisabled

members.name: name

members.name: relayNativeEvent

declarations.description:
**A switch is not a checkbox with a different shape.** A checkbox is an
answer to a question the form asks when it is submitted; a switch is a thing
happening now. That is why `role="switch"` exists and why a switch belongs
outside a form as often as in one: it says "on" and "off" rather than
"ticked" and "unticked", and a reader expects the effect immediately rather
than on Save.

Rendered as a real `<input type="checkbox">` carrying `role="switch"`, which
is the pairing ARIA describes: the input is what a form submits and what a
label forwards a press to, and the role is what a screen reader announces.
Neither half can be got from the other.

The label sits beside it, inside the `<label>` that forwards the press, the
way a checkbox's does. The hint and the message go under the row, because
there is no above: the switch and the words naming it are one line.

declarations.summary: One cell of a table.

declarations.description:
A column is a heading and a width, declared together, because they are two
facts about one thing and keeping them apart is what went wrong before.

**This replaces a `columns` string on the table.** That property took a CSS
track list, so the headings lived in a row of cells and the widths lived in
an attribute, and nothing tied the two together: a table with three headings
and a two-track list rendered without complaint. Worse, handing it the
headings instead of a track list produced invalid CSS, which the grid
silently ignored, so the whole table collapsed into one column and every cell
stacked. That happened, in this library's own example, and the failure said
nothing at all.

Now the column is the source of both. Add one and the table has another
track; remove one and it does not.

**It generates no box of its own**, the same as a row: the heading is a grid
item of the table, so it lines up with the cells under it rather than sitting
in a wrapper that has to be kept the same width.
declarations.name: HelixBaseTableColumn

members.name: width
members.description:
The track this column takes, as CSS.

A single track value, so anything valid in `grid-template-columns` works:
`16rem`, `auto`, `minmax(0, 2fr)`. Left unset the column shares what is
left over equally, which is `minmax(0, 1fr)` rather than `1fr`: a bare
`1fr` track keeps an automatic minimum and refuses to shrink under a long
cell, so one unbreakable value pushes the table past its container.

declarations.description:
A grid rather than a `<table>`, so every column lines up across rows while
each row stays a real element that can be styled, hidden, or made
interactive. Table layout gives column alignment and takes away almost
everything else; grid gives both.

table to anyone reading it. `table`, `row`, `cell`, and `columnheader` are
all set explicitly, and rows are `display: contents` so their cells become
items of the one grid that does the aligning.

members.description:

moment it has one. A raw track list is the right shape for the value and
the wrong place for it: the headings and the widths were two halves of one
fact held in two places, and nothing checked that they agreed. Worse, the
value is CSS, so handing it headings by mistake produced an invalid track
list, which a grid ignores in silence: the table collapsed to one column

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description:
Nothing is assigned by name, so the columns can be put in a row.

`role="columnheader"` was landing directly under `role="table"` with no
owning `row`, which is invalid: the table pattern is `table > row >
columnheader`, and a header cell with no row is a cell belonging to
nothing. The columns are ordinary children the consumer writes with no
`slot`, so the only way to put a wrapper around them without changing what
a consumer writes is to assign them here.

consumer's own markup, which is the change a React consumer's hydration
reports and does not patch up. Assignment writes nothing at all.

Safe against the server because this repo ships no declarative shadow DOM:
the shadow root exists only after upgrade, and the assignment below runs in
that same update. There is no window in which the shadow is present and the
assignment has not happened.

members.name: appearance
members.description:
How the row reads.

Unset is a raised pill on the selected tab with nothing behind the row,
which is what a set sitting inside other chrome wants. `underline` is a
rule under the row and a thicker one under the selected tab, for a set that
heads a page. `toggle` puts the pill in a framed, sunken track, which reads
as one control rather than as a row.

consumer's server markup does not already have.

members.description: Watches for anything that moves a tab, since none of it is a property.

members.name: sync
members.description: Pushes the current value down to whichever tab and panel own it.

members.name: watch
members.description:
Watches every tab for a change of size.

Called again whenever the set changes, because `tabs` reads `this.children`
and filters on `instanceof`, so it is empty until the tab elements upgrade.
At `firstUpdated` it frequently is empty, and observing nothing is silent.

`observe` is idempotent per element, so re-running this costs nothing and
needs no bookkeeping about which tabs are already watched.

members.name: handleSlotChange
members.description:
The set changed: pair it up, watch it, and measure it.

All three, where this used to be `sync()` alone, and the missing `place()`
is why an indicator could stay unplaced for the life of the page. The order
of events is what does it: the host renders and measures before its tabs
have upgraded, so there is no selected tab to measure and `place` refuses;
the ResizeObserver's one initial callback lands in that same gap; and then
the tabs upgrade, `slotchange` pairs them, nothing measures, and nothing
ever will again, because the host's size never changes.

Invisible in every example, because a tab strip that is only tabs is
exactly as tall as its tabs, so a mark at the top of the strip is a mark on
the tab. It showed up where something gives the strip a height of its own.

members.name: onActiveChange
members.description: The consumer's callback, invoked after the change is applied.

members.name: active
members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Called `active`, which is what this mixin is named for and what it was
not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

members.name: defaultActive
members.description: Initial item for uncontrolled use. Ignored once `active` is written.

members.name: activeState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: activeMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `active` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: requestActive
members.description:
Requests a new current item, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Unlike a native control, nothing has moved
by the time this runs, so refusing is simply not writing: there is
nothing to put back.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:

The first enabled one when `value` names nothing, which is a set before
its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.description:
A tag is a label, and optionally a label the reader can take off.
`dismissible` is what separates it from a badge: a badge reports a state the
reader cannot change, a tag names something they can.

Dismissing is a request. The tag does not remove itself, because the consumer
owns the list it sits in and taking the node out from under them would put
their state and the document out of step. Cancelling `helix-dismiss` is a
refusal.

declarations.description:
A real `<textarea>`, so the caret, the selection, spellcheck, the resize
handle and the keyboard a phone chooses are all the platform's, and it
serializes into the server's markup so the field is usable before any script
loads.

**Not an Input with a taller box.** The difference is the Enter key: in a
single-line field it submits the form, and here it inserts a line. That is a
behavioral difference the platform owns and cannot be styled into existence,
which is why this is its own element rather than `Input` with a property.

`rows` sets the height it starts at, and `auto-grow` lets it follow its own
content. They are not alternatives: `rows` is where an empty field begins and
`auto-grow` is what happens after, so a field that grows still has to start
somewhere.
declarations.name: HelixBaseTextarea

members.name: autoGrow
members.description: Whether the box follows its own content rather than scrolling.

members.name: placeholder
members.description: Shown while the field is empty. Not a label: it goes when typing starts.

members.name: readOnly
members.description: Whether the field refuses input while still submitting its value.

members.name: rows
members.description: How many lines the box is before anything is typed.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Focus is delegated to the control, so the host is never the target.

members.name: handleInput
members.description:
Every keystroke, cancelable, and put back where it is refused.

The control has already taken the character by the time this runs, so
refusing has to restore it, or what is on screen and what the form would
submit disagree.

members.name: handleChange
members.description: Relayed, because `change` does not cross a shadow boundary on its own.

members.name: grow
members.description:
Follows the content, by measuring rather than by counting.

`scrollHeight` is what the text actually needs, which no arithmetic over
line count and line height gets right: a wrapped line, a pasted paragraph
and a font that has not loaded yet all break the arithmetic and none of
them break the measurement.

Reset to `auto` first, because `scrollHeight` of an element already sized to
its content is that size, so without the reset the box can only ever grow.

members.name: resize
members.description:
Re-measures when the box changes rather than only when a property does.

The height was computed on Lit updates alone, and nothing about a container
narrowing, a font swapping, or the field finally gaining a layout box is a
property change here. A field that wrapped to three lines at one width kept
a three-line height at half the width and clipped the rest behind
`overflow: hidden`, with no way for a reader to reach it.

Observing the control also covers the zero case above from the other side:
a `ResizeObserver` fires when an element gains a box, so a field that was
hidden when it first tried to grow measures itself the moment it is shown.

members.name: focus
members.description: Puts the caret in the field, the way a label pointing at one would.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the value and the validity the host stands behind.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: onValueChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the value is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. `onValueChange` and not `onChange`,
because React reserves the latter for its own synthetic system and wires
it to the native `change`, so a Helix event named `Change` would never
fire at all.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description: The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

declarations.summary: Several lines of text a reader types into.

declarations.description:
An element rather than a slot, because it carries a timeout, a severity, a
dismiss control and a lifetime that pauses: behavior, state and API, which
is the test for whether a region becomes an element in this library.

**The timer is the item's own.** Held by the region, one message arriving
would restart another's, so a stack of three would go from three seconds each
to nine for the last one. Each message is on its own clock from the moment it
is rendered.

**A message is the opposite of the page it is over.** Inverted by default,
because a thing arriving in a corner has to be told apart from the page in
the moment before it is read, and inverting does that without spending a
color that means something. It is a flip of `color-scheme` rather than a
named inverse surface: every token in the subtree re-resolves, so a `Retry`
a consumer slots in comes out right without knowing where it is. `Tooltip`
can name the inverse surface directly because it holds no controls; this
cannot. Set `data-color-mode` on the region to take the page's mode instead.

**No duration means it stays.** That is the safe default rather than the
common one: anything carrying an action has to still be there when the reader
decides to take it, and a component cannot tell from the outside whether the
message it was given is disposable.

**The clock stops while it is being read.** Hover pauses it, and so does
focus landing anywhere inside, which is the case that matters more: a
keyboard reader tabbing towards the action in a toast is exactly the person a
timer must not race. Both resume where they left off rather than starting
again, so a message half-read does not get a full second life every time a
pointer crosses it.

**Going away is a request, never an act.** It dispatches a cancelable
`helix-dismiss` and does nothing else: the consumer owns the list, so the
item removing itself would leave the two disagreeing. Auto-dismiss and the
dismiss control raise the same event, so a consumer handles one path and not
two.
declarations.name: HelixBaseToastItem

members.name: duration
members.description:
How long it stays, in milliseconds. Absent means until it is dismissed.

Read once when the item is first rendered. Changing it afterwards does not
restart a message the reader is already partway through.

members.name: severity
members.description: What kind of message it is, which picks the mark and its name.

members.name: startedAt
members.description: When the current run of the timer began, or nothing while it is paused.

members.name: remaining
members.description: What is left of the duration, so resuming continues rather than restarts.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the message is still showing.

The same decide-once contract every other stateful thing here carries, and
it was the one exception: this waited to be told in every case, so
`duration` did nothing at all without consumer script and the dismiss
control looked broken to anyone who pressed it. `Dialog` closes itself,
`Accordion` closes itself, and there was no reason a message should not.

Declared by the markup and it is the consumer's: the item announces and
waits. Not declared and it is the item's: it goes when it is asked to, and
the consumer still hears `helix-dismiss` and takes it out of their own
list. Read once, at the first update.

**No `default-open`, unlike the four mixins.** A `default-` seed exists so
markup can choose a starting state without claiming ownership, and there is
only one starting state that makes sense: a message that has been rendered
is showing. An attribute whose only legal value is the default is an
attribute nobody can use.

members.name: openState
members.description: Whether it is showing, whoever said so, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: openMode
members.description: Whether the consumer owns it, decided once and then fixed.

members.name: dismiss
members.description:
Asks to be taken away, and reports whether the request stood.

Announced before anything happens, so `preventDefault()` is a refusal and
the message stays. The event still carries the label, because a consumer
removing this from their own state has to know which one went, and that is
true whether or not the item hid itself first.

members.name: pause
members.description: Stops the clock, leaving whatever is left of it.

members.name: resume
members.description: Starts it again from where it stopped.

members.name: holds
members.description:
How many reasons there are to hold the clock, rather than whether there is
one.

Hover and focus both stopped the same timer with nothing counting them, so
a reader who tabbed into a message and then moved the pointer off it had
the clock restarted underneath them while they were still reading it. That
is the case the pause exists for, and it was the case that broke it.

The two are genuinely independent: a pointer can leave while focus stays,
and focus can leave while the pointer stays. Only the last one out starts
it again.

members.name: dismissible
members.description: Whether it offers a control to take it away.

members.name: dismissLabel
members.description:

`attribute` is spelled out because Lit lowercases a property name to
derive one rather than dash-casing it, so this would otherwise be
reachable only as `dismisslabel`, which nobody would guess and no linter
would catch.

only things that do are a press and a timer.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

has to remember to include it.

events.description: Fired when it asks to go, whether by the control or by its timer.
events.name: helix-dismiss

attributes.name: duration
attributes.description:
How long it stays, in milliseconds. Absent means until it is dismissed.

Read once when the item is first rendered. Changing it afterwards does not
restart a message the reader is already partway through.

attributes.name: severity
attributes.description: What kind of message it is, which picks the mark and its name.

attributes.name: open
attributes.description:
Whether the message is still showing.

The same decide-once contract every other stateful thing here carries, and
it was the one exception: this waited to be told in every case, so
`duration` did nothing at all without consumer script and the dismiss
control looked broken to anyone who pressed it. `Dialog` closes itself,
`Accordion` closes itself, and there was no reason a message should not.

Declared by the markup and it is the consumer's: the item announces and
waits. Not declared and it is the item's: it goes when it is asked to, and
the consumer still hears `helix-dismiss` and takes it out of their own
list. Read once, at the first update.

**No `default-open`, unlike the four mixins.** A `default-` seed exists so
markup can choose a starting state without claiming ownership, and there is
only one starting state that makes sense: a message that has been rendered
is showing. An attribute whose only legal value is the default is an
attribute nobody can use.

attributes.name: dismissible
attributes.description: Whether it offers a control to take it away.

attributes.name: dismiss-label
attributes.description:
Accessible name for that control.

`attribute` is spelled out because Lit lowercases a property name to
derive one rather than dash-casing it, so this would otherwise be
reachable only as `dismisslabel`, which nobody would guess and no linter
would catch.

declarations.summary: One message in the toast region.

declarations.description:
**The region is why this is one family rather than two.** A live region has
to be in the document *before* a message is put into it: assistive technology
subscribes to the region, and a region that arrives already holding its
message is frequently not announced at all. So the container is a part of the
family and not an arranger of complete things, which is the same reasoning
that puts `Radio.Group` inside its own family.

**Polite, never assertive.** `role="alert"` interrupts whatever a reader is
being told, and almost nothing that arrives in a corner of the screen has
earned that. Something that genuinely cannot wait is a `Dialog`, which stops
the page for everyone rather than only for the people who cannot see it.

**It never creates or destroys anything.** The consumer renders items and
removes them; asking to go is a cancelable `helix-dismiss` from the item.
That is still exactly true of the region: an item that has gone hides itself
and stays in the tree, so a consumer whose state still lists it does not have
their framework fighting a node this component took away. What changed is
that the item no longer waits to be told before hiding, unless the consumer
declared `open` and said the state is theirs.
There is no `toast.show()`, because an imperative queue inside a component is
a second copy of the application's state that nothing can render from: an app
that wants a `toast()` function writes a thin one over the state it already
has, and keeps the ability to render the same messages on the server, in a
test, or twice.

declarations.description:
The indicator is one element that travels, not a background that appears on
whichever item is current. That difference is the whole point: a fill that
swaps is two things changing at once and reads as a flicker, while one that
moves is a single object the eye follows, and it says where the selection
came from as well as where it went.

Its whole box is measured from the selected item and written onto
the indicator as custom properties, because labels are different lengths and
no proportion of the group is the right answer. Measurement is client-side by
necessity, so the server renders the indicator hidden and it fades in once it
has somewhere to be, which is the harmless direction: it appears rather than
jumping from a wrong place.

A radio group, and only that. Navigation is links marked with `aria-current`
and styled by the `data-nav-item` recipe: radio semantics would announce a
set of destinations as a set of choices. A tab controls a panel.

Being a radio group, it is a form control, and it says so through
`HelixFormElement`: it reports its value under a `name`, comes back to the
markup's choice on reset, and restores the one a reader made when the browser
brings a form back.

The semantics were already right: the host has carried `role="radiogroup"`
and the items `role="radio"` from the start. What none of it did was reach a
form. A button in a shadow root submits nothing whatever its role, so the
value has to be reported by the host, which is the only thing a form can
see.

members.name: sync
members.description:
Marks the chosen item, which used to happen inside the placing method.

They were one method because the geometry needed the active item anyway,
and that made a selection change look like a layout concern. `resolveActiveItem`
rather than the first item, because a group opening on a disabled segment
marked it as chosen.

members.name: indicator
members.default: new IndicatorController(this, { // The same exact match `sync` makes: nothing chosen means nothing marked, // and the controller takes the mark away rather than parking it on item one. active: () => this.items.find((item) => item.value === this.value), indicator: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="indicator"]'), surface: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="track"]'), })

members.name: watch
members.description:
Watches the group and every item it currently holds.

Called again on `slotchange`, because the set was read once at first paint:
an item added later was measured by nothing, so a group whose options
arrive with the data had a thumb that stopped following the moment one of
them changed width. Observing the same element twice is a no-op, so there
is nothing to unwind first.

members.name: validate
members.description:
The verdict on the answer, which `required` had been asking for and not
getting.

`required` arrived with `MixinField` and nothing enforced it: the attribute
reflected, the marker rendered beside the label, and a form with an
unanswered group submitted anyway. An API that exists and does nothing is
worse than one that is missing, because the marker is a promise to the
reader that something will stop them.

The anchor is the track rather than the host, so the browser's own bubble
points at the control rather than at a box with nothing in it.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: onValueChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the value is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. `onValueChange` and not `onChange`,
because React reserves the latter for its own synthetic system and wires
it to the native `change`, so a Helix event named `Change` would never
fire at all.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description: The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

declarations.description:
Separate from a button group, and the difference is what it holds: a group is
homogeneous, a toolbar is not. A toolbar mixes buttons, toggles, and menus,
which is why it is its own component rather than a variant of something.

The whole toolbar is one tab stop and the arrows move between controls, so a
page with three toolbars costs three presses of Tab to get past rather than
thirty. Controls are found by asking the browser what is focusable rather
than by matching tag names, so a toolbar works with anything put in it,
including a consumer's own elements.

a toolbar holds anything, including elements this package has never heard
of. Client only: there is no tree to walk on the server.

members.name: setTabStop
members.description:
Moves the single tab stop to one control.

The attribute is a change to markup the consumer rendered, which a React
consumer's hydration reports and does not patch up; a control that offers
the property moves the stop inside its own shadow root instead.

members.name: claimTabStop
members.description:

A custom element has no properties at all before it upgrades, so a pass
that ran first would find no `focusable`, take the `tabindex` fallback, and
write the very attribute this exists to avoid.

members.name: restoreTabStop
members.description:

holding the stop dropped it out of the list while every other control was
already at `-1`. The toolbar then had no tab stop at all and the keyboard
could not reach it again, from a change as ordinary as a Save button
disabling itself once the form is clean.

has never heard of that was never given `tabindex="-1"` is still in the
document's own tab order, so it is never the one that gets stranded.

members.name: axis
members.description:

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on

makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what

name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native

declarations.description:
The trigger is slotted and stays the consumer's own element. The bubble is
rendered here, in the top layer through the popover API, so it clears any
ancestor with `overflow: hidden` without a `z-index` anywhere.

Position comes from `FloatingController`, which flips to another side when
the preferred one does not fit and slides along it to stay in view.

**The description is linked by element reference, not by id.** An IDREF
cannot cross a shadow boundary, so `aria-describedby` on a slotted trigger
pointing at a bubble in here resolves to nothing.
`ElementInternals.ariaDescribedByElements` takes the element itself, which
does cross.

It shows on hover and on focus, and hides on leave, on blur, and on Escape.
A tooltip that answers only the pointer is one a keyboard reader never sees.

The pointer waits out `delay` first, or sweeping a row of controls flashes a
tooltip for each of them. Focus does not wait: a keyboard reader landing on a
control has already committed to it.

Open state comes from `MixinControllerOpen`, so it announces `helix-open` and
`helix-close` like every other overlay here, and a consumer can drive it with
`open` where they need to.

members.description:

members.name: delay
members.description:
How long the pointer must rest before the bubble appears, in milliseconds.

Without one, sweeping across a row of controls flashes a tooltip for each
of them, which is noise rather than help. Focus opens with no delay: a

members.description: How long the bubble stays after the pointer leaves, in milliseconds.

members.name: holds
members.description:

nothing counting them, so whichever left last won: moving the pointer off a
control that still had keyboard focus scheduled a hide and took the bubble
away from under the reader. The same fault the toast timer had, and the

members.description:

members.name: hasContent
members.description: Whether there is anything to show. Asked of the slot rather than of the property, because either can carry the content. `assignedNodes` without `flatten` answers what the consumer provided and not what the fallback would render, which is exactly the question: a bubble with only fallback and an empty property is empty. An element on its own would count ` ` as something to say, and text on its own would count an icon as nothing, when an icon is the whole point of slotting rather than setting the property. members.name: handleContentChange
members.description:

members.description: Hides the bubble.

members.name: hideLater
members.description: Hides after `delayOut`, so crossing the gap to the bubble does not close it.

members.name: release
members.description: Hides only once nothing is holding the bubble up.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
Escape closes the bubble from wherever the reader is.

element and Escape worked only for the one case that needed it least. That

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: onOpenChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the state is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. And not reachable from React's JSX,
which reserves every `on[A-Z]` prop for its own event system and drops
what it does not recognize; the generated wrapper listens for the events
instead.

element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

declarations.description:
**`open`, on `MixinControllerOpen`, where it was a bare `expanded` boolean.**
A branch showing its children is the same state a disclosure holds, and
`AccordionItem` has been on that mixin all along. Written here by hand it had
neither half of what the mixin gives: `this.expanded = !this.expanded`
announced nothing, so a consumer could not know a branch had opened, and
could not own the state either. `aria-expanded` is still what the row
renders, because that is the attribute a tree uses; the property is what
changed, not the semantics.

whether it is selected, and whether it is the one holding focus.

A branch is any item with something slotted into `children`, detected in
`firstUpdated` rather than declared by the consumer. That is a client-side
enhancement by necessity, since the server cannot inspect children, so the
server renders the node as a leaf and the twisty appears on hydration. It
appears rather than disappearing, which is the harmless direction.

declarations.summary: One node in a tree.

declarations.description:
Focus is a single tab stop, moved with the arrow keys, which is what the tree
pattern requires: a sidebar of forty items should not be forty presses of Tab
to get past. The tree owns which item is the tab stop and moves it as focus
moves, so the browser's own focus order is never fought with.

Items are found with `instanceof`, never by tag name, so the headless tier
does not learn about the styled one.

members.name: chevron
members.description:
Which end of a row the chevron sits at.

Unset is the start, which is what a tree of folders looks like. `end` puts
it at the far side, where it reads as a control belonging to the row rather
than as part of the name, and it lets every label start at one place
without a row that has no chevron reserving space for one.

On the tree rather than on each item, because a row whose chevron sat
somewhere different from its siblings' would be a mistake, not a choice.

members.description: Accessible name for the tree.

members.description: Every item, in the order a reader moving down would meet them.

members.name: visibleItems
members.description: Items a reader can actually reach: not inside a collapsed branch.

members.name: syncItems
members.description:
Pushes tree-owned state down: which item is selected, which holds the tab
stop, and how deep each one sits.

Depth is computed here rather than by each item counting its own ancestors,
so an item moved in the tree gets the right indent without knowing it moved.

members.name: handleBranch
members.description:
A branch opened or closed, whoever did it.

The keyboard paths called `syncItems` by hand and the pointer path did not,
so collapsing a branch by clicking its chevron left the tab stop on a row
inside the subtree that had just been hidden: the tree kept its one stop
and the stop was on something nobody could see or reach. Listening for the
item's own open events covers every way a branch can move, including a
consumer setting `open` directly.

members.name: active
members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

members.description: Initial item for uncontrolled use. Ignored once `active` is written.

members.name: activeState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: activeMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `active` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: requestActive
members.description:
Requests a new current item, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Unlike a native control, nothing has moved
by the time this runs, so refusing is simply not writing: there is
nothing to put back.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:
Which item is current, given what there is to choose from.

The first enabled one when `value` names nothing, which is a set before
its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

events.description: Fired before the current node moves, and cancelable. The only way to refuse one.
events.name: helix-change

events.description: Fired when an item is chosen. Dispatched by the item and listened for here, because the tree is what a consumer holds a reference to.
events.name: helix-select

attributes.name: chevron
attributes.description:
Which end of a row the chevron sits at.

Unset is the start, which is what a tree of folders looks like. `end` puts
it at the far side, where it reads as a control belonging to the row rather
than as part of the name, and it lets every label start at one place
without a row that has no chevron reserving space for one.

On the tree rather than on each item, because a row whose chevron sat
somewhere different from its siblings' would be a mistake, not a choice.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the tree.

attributes.name: active
attributes.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Called `active`, which is what this mixin is named for and what it was
not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

attributes.name: default-active
attributes.description: Initial item for uncontrolled use. Ignored once `active` is written.

declarations.summary: A tree of items, navigable entirely from the keyboard.
